# How to work in `estate-agent`

The standard for AI agents working across a repo estate. One context file per repo that every assistant reads, a cross-repo service map built from contracts rather than parsers, guardrails that block credential access, and a repair loop that keeps it all true.

## What you are allowed to do here

**Tier 2 — Reviewed.** In this repo you may edit code and open pull requests. You may not merge anything - every change needs passing CI and a human reviewer.

_Why this tier: the normal setting for a service with tests and a review process._

## Never do these

- Add a dependency. Zero dependencies is what makes this installable on a locked-down work laptop and what keeps docs/data-flow.md verifiable in a minute. tests/test_no_network.py fails the build if one appears.
- Add network code of any kind, including telemetry, update checks or analytics. The no-network claim is load-bearing and enforced by a test.
- Overwrite something a human wrote. Generated files carry a content hash so a hand edit is distinguishable from a stale file; hand edits are preserved and offered for promotion, never clobbered.
- Loosen a safety rule automatically. Auto-tuning may suggest; only a person applies. Automated changes tighten or report, never widen.
- Put anything identifying into this repo - company names, internal hostnames, employee names, real credentials. Your estate shapes the detection patterns, never the names. Enforced over files and git history.
- Confuse levels with tiers. A level is how far someone has adopted (0-4); a tier is what one repo lets an agent do (1-3). They are numbered separately on purpose.
- Make the CLI punny. The project name is a joke; `estate scan` and `estate init` are not.

## Commands

| Purpose | Command |
| --- | --- |
| test | `python3 tests/run_all.py` |
| lint | `python3 tests/test_publishable.py` |
| report | `python3 tests/run_all.py --report` |
| site | `python3 site/build.py` |

## Conventions

- Precision over recall, everywhere. A phantom connection is worse than a missing one: a missed connection gets added by hand and stays added, while one false alarm stops the whole map being trusted. When in doubt, ask a question rather than emit an edge.
- Every claim carries its evidence. An edge cites file:line and records how it was resolved. If it cannot be evidenced, it does not ship.
- Never silently truncate, skip or drop. A cap that hides what it dropped produces confident wrong answers; report it instead. Several real bugs here were silent drops.
- A check that cries wolf is worse than no check. False positives get the guard switched off, and a switched-off guard protects nothing. Measure the false-positive rate, do not just assert it.
- Match the existing prose style in docs - plain language, no jargon without a definition, every doc opens with what it is for and stays under two pages.
- Python 3.9 is the floor. tests/test_python_compat.py enforces it.
- Comments explain why, not what. Where a rule exists because a real bug was found, say so - those comments are the reason the rule survives refactors.

## Architecture

```
A CLI over a scanner, with no server and no database.
  bin/estate            launcher; finds src/ next to itself, no install step
  src/estate_agent/
    cli.py              command dispatch; subcommands imported lazily
    yamlite.py          the YAML subset reader/writer (no PyYAML fallback,
                        deliberately - two parsers means the one you test is
                        not the one that runs)
    deed.py             .agent/estate.yaml: schema, validation, tiers
    render.py           deed -> five assistant files, with the drift stamp
    stacks.py           loads stacks/*.yaml; detection and classification
    discover.py         walks repos, extracts endpoints and call signals
    infra.py            shared clusters, caches, datastores
    graph.py            the resolution ladder; signals -> edges or questions
    impact.py           blast radius and landing order
    scan/doctor/initialise/upkeep/vault/report/contribute.py   commands
  stacks/*.yaml         one file per language; the whole extension model
  hooks/secret_guard.py single-file PreToolUse hook, copied into user repos
  tests/                run with `python3 tests/run_all.py`, no test runner
  site/                 stdlib generator for the GitHub Pages site
The resolution ladder in graph.py is the core idea: declared > dependency >
env > host > path, with anything ambiguous becoming a question. Read
docs/estate.md before changing it.
```

## If this file turns out to be wrong

These notes are generated from `.agent/estate.yaml`. They can go stale, and stale instructions are worse than none — you will act on them confidently and be wrong.

So if reality contradicts anything above — a command fails, a service named here no longer exists, an endpoint has been renamed — then as part of the same piece of work:

1. Fix `.agent/estate.yaml` (the source), **not this file** — edits here are overwritten.
2. Run `estate sync` to regenerate.
3. Mention the correction in your pull request description, in one line, so a human can sanity-check it.

Do not silently work around a wrong instruction. Correcting it is part of the task, and it is how these notes get better over time rather than worse.

## Notes

READ THIS FIRST IF YOU ARE AN AGENT PICKING UP WORK HERE.
What this project is for, in one line: an AI agent in one repo cannot see
the other ninety, and nothing stops it doing damage. Everything here exists
to fix one of those two problems, or to stop the fix going stale.
How to make a change well:
1. Run `python3 tests/run_all.py` first. 182 tests, seconds, no setup.
2. Read `docs/` for the area you are touching. The docs are the design; the
   code follows them, not the other way round.
3. For anything touching detection or resolution, run
   `python3 tests/run_all.py --report` before and after. Precision must stay
   at 100% on the fixture. Recall may improve; precision may not regress.
4. Field-test it. `docs/field-testing.md` lists the bugs found by running
   this against real repositories - performance, phantom edges, silent
   truncation, content loss. Every one was invisible by reading the code and
   obvious within a minute of running it. Reasoning about a scanner tells you
   almost nothing.
Adding a language is one YAML file in `stacks/` and no code. That is the
main way this project grows - see docs/adding-a-stack.md and
`estate contribute stack <repo>`, which scaffolds one from real code with
redaction applied.
The rules in `never_do` above are not style preferences. Each one is
load-bearing and most were learned the hard way; CONTRIBUTING.md explains
why for each.
